sense: with the hand, to someone arriving or leaving

terms.gloss: wave (to someone), make signs with a shaken hand
terms.grammar: ablative absolute concussā manū, with signa dare and the dative of the person; also manum concutere
evidence: Ov. Met. 11.465: concussāque manū dantem sibi signa marītum
Lewis & Short s.v. concutiō: manum, Ov. M. 11.465
terms.comment: Ovid’s picture of a husband waving from the stern of a ship, and of his wife waving back (redditque notās, “and returns the signs”). We have found no single classical verb for waving the hand; the phrase is plain enough to say, and manum concute will do for a child. Of the sea’s waves, see “wave”.

phrases.latin: Avō valē dīc, et manum concute.
phrases.english: Say goodbye to Grandpa, and wave.

phrases.latin: Ecce, avia nōbīs ē fenestrā manū signa dat!
phrases.english: Look, Grandma’s waving to us from the window!

phrases.latin: stantemque in puppe recurvā concussāque manū dantem sibi signa marītum prōna videt redditque notās
phrases.english: leaning forward, she sees her husband standing on the curved stern and waving to her, and she waves back

sources: Lewis & Short: concutio · Lewis & Short: signum
